summary: Correct basic idea (slalom pole on a sprung ground spike), but a flat yellow untextured cylinder with no cap, branding or wear; reads as CG at any distance.
critique: Silhouette is right: a long slender pole on a short black spring-and-spike base, and the rounded top is a reasonable cap. Proportions look plausible (roughly 1.6-1.8 m, about 25-32 mm diameter), though the pole reads slightly too thick-to-tall for a 25 mm pole, so check it against the 25-32 mm reference. Problems: (1) The albedo is one saturated mustard yellow with no gradient, no specular variation, no UV fade and no scuffing. Real PVC slalom poles are glossy fluorescent yellow (or orange/red/blue), slightly translucent at the edges, scuffed and grass-stained on the bottom 30 cm where boots and studs hit them. (2) There is no separate top cap. Real poles have a black or matching rubber end cap about 30 mm long that is visibly a different material. (3) The spring is a good touch, but the base is one dark grey material. Real spring bases have a bright zinc-plated or black-painted coil, a black plastic or rubber collar where the pole sits, and a sharpened galvanised steel spike that should show bare metal and soil dirt. (4) There is no contact with the ground: the spike should disappear into the turf with a small tuft or a disturbed-soil ring. (5) Up close the cylinder is visibly faceted at the top in the close view; use 12 sides minimum and smooth normals.
suggestions: Add a distinct end cap: a 30-40 mm long cylinder about 2 mm wider than the pole, black rubber (albedo ~0.04, roughness 0.7). About 24 tris.

Material: switch to a gloss PVC look (roughness 0.25-0.35, albedo a fluorescent yellow such as sRGB #E8D21A rather than the current mustard) and add a vertical-gradient dirt mask on the bottom 0.3 m (darken 20-30%, roughness up to 0.6) plus a few scuff streaks. A 64x256 tiling detail or vertex colours are enough.

Split the base into three materials: rubber collar (black, rough), zinc spring (metallic 1, roughness 0.35, light grey), and spike (bare steel tip with brown dirt on the lowest 5 cm). Sink the spike 100-150 mm into the ground plane so only the collar and the spring show.
Optional: a printed brand band or a 2-colour variant (yellow/black or red/white spiral tape) as a cheap decal for variety; offer 3-4 colour variants by tint.
Keep the total under ~300 tris; it can be instanced in rows of 10-20 on a training pitch.
renderer_notes: The pole reads darker and more orange on its shaded side because there is no bounce from the lawn (no GI); that is the renderer, not the asset.

summary: Recognisable generic hatchback with right overall proportions, but a toy-like soft blob with box mirrors, broken headlight decals, no grille, flush featureless glazing and no shut lines.
critique: Overall length-to-height ratio is about right for a Golf/Focus class car (side view ~2.9:1 against 4284x1456 for a Golf Mk8), and the wheelbase and wheel placement are roughly correct. Everything else lets it down. (1) The front end: the headlight decals render as jagged white and orange shards (an alpha or UV-cut error, or z-fighting with the body) and look broken in every view. There is no grille aperture, no lower intake, no badge and no fog-light recesses; the 'grille' is a flat grey rectangle on a smooth nose. The nose is long, low and rounded like a 1990s coupe. A modern hatch has a high, blunt bonnet leading edge and a tall, near-vertical front face. (2) Mirrors are unbevelled floating boxes on stalks, the single worst silhouette element. Real mirrors are teardrop housings ~250x150x120 mm on a short sail at the A-pillar base. (3) Glazing is a flat dark tint set flush into the body with no black DLO surround, no B-pillar blackout, no rubber seals and no reflection. The windscreen has no wiper cowl detail beyond two thin lines. (4) Body is a smooth soft blob with no character line along the doors, no wheel-arch lips, no shut lines with depth, and no visible sills or door-handle recesses (the handles are tiny dark ticks). (5) Rear: the tail lights are flat red boxes, the hatch has no spoiler, no rear wiper, no number-plate recess or lamp, and the bumper has no diffuser or reflectors. (6) Wheels: the 5-spoke rims are fine, but the tyres have no sidewall bulge or lettering, and the arches show no inner liner (a black arch cavity is visible but uniform). (7) Paint: a uniform matte-ish blue with no clearcoat. Car paint needs a clear sharp specular highlight; this reads as plastic.
suggestions: Fix the headlight decals first: they are the most visible defect. Model each lamp as a slightly recessed inset (5-10 mm) with a clear lens material over a chrome reflector and an LED DRL strip, rather than an alpha decal. About 60-100 tris per lamp.

Re-profile the front: raise the bonnet leading edge to ~750-800 mm, make the front face near-vertical, and cut a real grille opening (honeycomb or slat mesh on an alpha or normal-mapped plane) plus a lower intake. Add a badge decal.
Replace the box mirrors with teardrop housings (8-12 segments, ~150 tris each) on an A-pillar sail, body colour with a black base and a mirror-glass face.

Glazing: add a gloss black DLO band (40-60 mm) around every window, black-out the B-pillar, use a glass material (roughness 0.05, slight reflection or env-map, darker tint ~0.08 albedo) and inset the glass ~10 mm from the body surface.
Body detail via a normal map or real cuts: door shut lines (5 mm deep grooves), a shoulder character line, flared wheel-arch lips, and sills. Door handles as recessed 120 mm pull handles.
Paint: a clearcoat-like look (base roughness 0.35 plus low-roughness specular, or a single roughness ~0.2) and slight dirt on the lower 200 mm and behind the wheels.
Rear: wraparound tail lamps with an inner chevron pattern, a roof spoiler over the hatch glass, a rear wiper, a plate recess and a black lower diffuser with reflectors.

Tyres: add sidewall bulge (a slightly convex profile), a 225/45 R17 sized tyre, and lettering via the normal map. Budget the whole car at 6-10k tris with one 1k-2k atlas; it still instances well for a car park.
renderer_notes: The car is shadow-side dark at the doors because there is no GI or env reflection; a cubemap or sky-specular term would help all car paint. The broken headlight shards look like asset decal or UV issues, not the renderer.

summary: Reads as a 13 t tracked excavator from a distance, but it is a blocky toy: box cab with black panes, a black half-cylinder counterweight, hydraulic rams that float free of the boom, and no handrails, steps, hoses or cab framing.
critique: Layout is right (tracked undercarriage, slewing upper with offset cab on the left, boom on the right of the cab, exhaust stack, bucket with teeth), and the tracks have visible grouser shoes, which is the best part. Problems in priority order: (1) Hydraulics are wrong. The boom cylinders and the dipper (stick) cylinder are thin rods with ball ends that stick out past the boom and dipper rather than pinning into lugs on them. In the close view the stick cylinder sits above the boom knuckle and pokes into space. A Cat 313 has two boom cylinders (~140 mm bore, chrome rods) pinned to the upper frame below the boom foot, one stick cylinder on top of the boom, and a bucket cylinder on top of the stick driving an H-link and dogbone at the bucket. None of the linkage near the bucket is modelled. (2) Boom and stick proportions: the stick is very long and nearly vertical, and the boom is a uniform-section box. Real booms are a curved banana shape, deeper at the knuckle (~600 mm) and tapering to ~350 mm, with welded side plates. Stick length for a 313 is ~2.5-3.0 m against a ~4.6 m boom. (3) Cab: a plain yellow box with flat black rectangles. A real ROPS cab has black pillars, large framed glass on the front, side and door, a roof guard, wipers and a door handle, and it sits ~1 m above the track top. (4) The counterweight is a black half-cylinder that reads as a separate object. On a 313 it is a body-coloured, rounded-back casting with a Cat-style taillight recess, and it continues the upper house line. (5) The upper house is a single box with a flat lid. It needs engine hood panels with louvre grilles, a side service door, handrails along the right deck, steps on the track frame, and mirrors. (6) Undercarriage: no visible sprocket teeth or idler, no carrier rollers, no track guards. The track frame is a flat block. (7) Materials: flat saturated yellow everywhere, with no decals (model number, warning stripes), no mud on the tracks and lower boom, no chrome on the cylinder rods, and no paint wear at the bucket and teeth.
suggestions: Rebuild the hydraulics as proper cylinders: barrel (yellow or black, ~180 mm OD) plus chrome rod (~80 mm, metallic 1, roughness 0.15), each pinned between modelled lugs on the frame, boom, stick and bucket link. Add the bucket H-link and dogbone. ~1.5k tris total.

Reshape the boom as a curved, tapered box section (deeper at the knuckle) and set the stick to ~0.6x the boom length. Pose the default as a typical parked pose: bucket curled on the ground in front of the tracks.

Cab: a framed ROPS cab with black pillars (~60 mm), tinted glass (roughness 0.05, albedo ~0.05), a front wiper, a roof guard and a door outline. Put the operator seat and joysticks behind the glass for close-ups (a few hundred tris).
Counterweight: body-yellow rounded rear casting matching the house radius, with a recessed rear work light and a 'CAT 313'-style but brand-neutral decal.
Upper house: split into engine hood with louvre normal-map grilles, a right-side service door, yellow handrails (30 mm tube) along the deck, and grab handles plus 2-3 steps down to the track frame.

Undercarriage: add a drive sprocket with teeth at the rear, a front idler, 1-2 carrier rollers on top, bottom rollers, and track guards. Keep the track shoes as a tiled normal-mapped strip, not individual meshes, if the budget is tight.

Materials: Cat-yellow albedo ~sRGB #E8A90F with roughness 0.5, mud and dust masks on the tracks and lower 0.5 m (brown, roughness 0.9), bucket wear exposing bare steel at the cutting edge and teeth, black and yellow chevron warning decals on the counterweight. Target 12-20k tris with a 2k atlas; it is a hero machine on a site, not a hundred-instance prop.
renderer_notes: The black counterweight and black cab panes read as holes partly because there is no sky reflection on glossy or dark surfaces; still, these are material choices in the asset.

summary: Best of this batch: correct round-top frame, mesh, couplers and rubber feet at roughly the right 3.5 x 2.0 m size, but the mesh is too coarse, the materials are a flat grey, and it lacks the clamp, stay and wear details that sell it.
critique: Proportions look right (about 3.5 m wide by 2.0 m tall, round-top upper corners, straight bottom rail). The frame tube reads as ~38 mm round, and the panel stands in two feet with the legs dropped into them, which is how real Heras sits. Shortfalls: (1) Mesh density: the render shows roughly 22-25 vertical wires and 9-10 horizontal wires. Typical UK anti-climb Heras mesh is about 75 mm x 300 mm (verticals every ~75 mm, so ~45 across 3.4 m) or 60 x 200 mm on standard panels. The current grid looks like a playground panel. The wires also render as bright white aliased lines in sunlight and near-black on the other face; real galvanised wire reads mid grey with a dull sheen. (2) Couplers are plain grey cubes on the top corners. Real Heras couplers are cast or pressed steel clamps (two half-shells with a single M12 bolt and nut) fitted between two panels at top and bottom, and a lone panel would usually show no coupler or show one hanging. (3) Feet: dark grey slabs. Real Heras feet are recycled black rubber or concrete-filled plastic blocks, ~700 x 200 x 140 mm, with chamfered edges, two leg holes and moulded ribs or a recycled-rubber speckle. Here they look flat-topped and featureless. (4) Material: one uniform grey with no galvanised spangle, white zinc oxide, rust at welds, mud on the bottom rail, or cable ties. (5) No mesh weld nodes or welded frame junctions; the wires simply end at the frame. (6) Missing the most common accessory: a support stay or the attached fence-banner or 'Danger: Construction Site' sign that most site panels carry.
suggestions: Increase mesh density to ~75 x 300 mm (about 45 verticals x 6-7 horizontals) and render the mesh as an alpha-tested texture on two quads (or one double-sided quad) instead of geometry. That is cheaper than now (2-4 tris plus a 512x512 tiling alpha, mipmapped with alpha-to-coverage) and kills the aliasing.

Wire and frame material: galvanised steel, albedo ~0.55 grey, metallic 1, roughness 0.45-0.55, with a mottled spangle/zinc-bloom detail map and a brown rust and mud mask on the bottom rail and the leg ends.
Feet: model as 700x200x140 mm chamfered blocks with two leg holes and a ribbed top (normal map), black recycled rubber (albedo 0.05, roughness 0.9) with faint speckle. ~60 tris each.

Couplers: replace cubes with two-half clamp shapes plus a bolt head and nut (~80 tris), dull galvanised; place them only where panels join, or one at top and bottom on the right edge to mate with the next panel.

Add optional variants: an anti-climb panel, a panel with a debris-netting or printed hoarding banner (one quad with alpha), a panel with a site-safety sign zip-tied on, and an angled support stay to a third foot.
Add a slight random lean (0.5-1.5 deg) and foot rotation per instance in placement so runs of fence do not look laser-straight.
renderer_notes: The mesh flicking between bright white and near-black depending on view side is partly back-face lighting in the forward renderer; ensure double-sided normals are flipped for the back face or render the mesh as a two-sided alpha card with consistent normals.

summary: Reasonable shrub foliage in a plain grey trough; the box is an untextured featureless shell and the shrub has visible stretched alpha-card smears, so it reads as a simple CG prop.
critique: The shrub is the stronger half. In the top-down close view the leaf cards read as individual leaves with colour variation, which is good. In the side and three-quarter views, though, several cards are viewed edge-on and render as stretched streaky smears (most visible on the left and right of the mound), and the mound shape is a symmetric dome with a hollow on one side rather than a natural clipped box or pittosporum. The planter trough has the right idea (a lipped rectangular trough, roughly 1.2 x 0.6 x 0.5 m) but: (1) the material is a uniform light grey with no texture. Real street planters are GRP with a fine stone-effect finish, cast concrete with aggregate and form-tie marks, or Corten or powder-coated steel, and all show water staining, soil stains below the lip and dirt at the base. (2) Geometry is a perfectly sharp box with a thin lip and no base plinth, no feet or drainage gap, and no bevels; the corners catch no highlight. (3) Soil is a flat brown plane with no mulch, bark chip, pebbles or uneven surface, and it sits close to the rim with no visible inner wall depth. (4) No grounding: the trough sits on the lawn with no contact darkening.
suggestions: Fix the shrub cards: orient cards to face outward from the mound centre (normals from a sphere) and fade alpha for cards viewed edge-on, or use cross-quads so no card is ever seen at a grazing angle. Add some branch geometry visible at the base.
Make the mound less symmetric: 3-5 overlapping lumps of varied size, slight overhang past the rim on one side, and a darker interior (vertex AO) so the shrub has depth.

Trough geometry: 10-20 mm bevels on all edges, a recessed 30-50 mm plinth or four short feet, and a slightly thicker rim (60-80 mm) with an inner wall visible 50-80 mm down to the soil. Still under 300 tris.

Trough material: pick one real type and texture it. For cast concrete use a 512 tiling map with aggregate speckle, roughness 0.85, albedo ~0.45; add vertical water streaks below the lip and a dark soil splash band at the bottom via a second UV or vertex colour.
Soil: replace the flat brown with bark mulch or a pebble-dressed surface (normal map plus albedo, 256 tiling), lowered 60 mm below the rim, with a few fallen leaves.
Offer variants: round planter, Corten steel trough, timber-clad planter, and seasonal plantings (box ball, lavender, ornamental grasses) by swapping the foliage cluster.
renderer_notes: The shadowed side of the trough goes near-black because there is no sky bounce or GI; a brighter sky ambient term would help but the flat untextured grey is the asset's own problem.

summary: Broken assembly: the rail, seat pan, backrest and lower bar float apart and are rotated on different axes, so it does not read as a rail seat at all.
critique: In every view the parts are disconnected. A thick chrome rail floats well above the seat, the backrest and seat-pan panels hang in mid-air with a gap between them and no mounting, a second short tube sits below and behind the lower panel, and from the side view the pieces are tilted on different axes (the top rail tips toward the camera and the panels are offset). This looks like per-part transforms being applied in the wrong space (for example a fold or pivot rotation applied around the world origin instead of each part's hinge, or an offset applied twice). Even ignoring the assembly bug, the parts are flat rectangles: a real rail seat (the safe-standing type used in UK grounds) is a moulded polypropylene tip-up seat with a contoured pan and back, a vertical steel post or bracket bolted to the riser, and a horizontal galvanised or powder-coated rail at ~1.1 m height on top of the back, with the seat folded up and locked against the post in standing mode. The materials are a glossy candy red with a mirror-chrome rail, which reads as plastic toy rather than UV-stable stadium polypropylene and powder-coated steel.
suggestions: First fix the assembly bug: check the transform order for the rail, back, pan and lower bar (likely the pivot or fold rotation is applied around the wrong origin or in world space). The pan hinge should sit on the post at ~430-450 mm height, the back top at ~800-850 mm, and the rail must sit directly on top of the post at ~1100 mm, all touching. Add a test that the parts' bounding boxes overlap or touch.

Model the structure: one vertical post per seat (60x40 mm RHS or a 48 mm tube) bolted to a base plate at the riser, the horizontal rail (48-60 mm tube, powder-coated black or grey, roughness 0.5, not mirror chrome) running across seats, and a hinge bracket for the pan.

Shape the seat parts: a contoured moulded pan ~450 mm wide with a front roll and two ribs on the underside, a curved backrest ~350 mm tall with a lip, both ~25-40 mm thick at the edges. 300-600 tris per seat, using LODs because there are thousands.
Material: polypropylene in club colours with roughness 0.45-0.55 (not glossy), a slight fade or chalky UV bloom on top surfaces, seat-number decals on the back or pan, and scuffs on the front edge.
Provide both states (pan down for sitting, pan up locked for safe standing) as two meshes or a single pivot so the stand can mix them.
renderer_notes: The strong specular hot-spots on the red panels and the mirror chrome rail exaggerate the toy look; part is a low roughness value in the asset, part is the lack of environment reflection in the renderer.

summary: The desert layout is pitch, box goals and corner flags only (by design, per layouts/desert.json). The circle mow and goalmouth wear are convincing, but the turf is flat and uniform at grazing angles and the pitch meets the farmland with no surround.
critique: Only this part can be judged: layouts/desert.json defines only pitch (bermuda grass, circle mowing, wear 0.15), box-style goals with a checker hex net, and striped corner flags. There are no stands, roof, facade, floodlights, dugouts or boards in this layout, so those parts are not scored. What works: the circular mow pattern reads well from the overall high views, the line markings are crisp, straight and the right width, the goal-mouth wear patches are a nice touch, and the box goal frame looks correct at 7.32 x 2.44 m with a hex net. Problems: (1) At low grazing angles (detail views 1 and 3) the turf becomes a flat, uniform light-green plane with no blade texture, no colour variation and no specular sheen. Real bermuda in hot climates is a distinct yellow-blue-green, finer and denser, and shows strong grain-direction light/dark contrast under a circle mow. (2) The wear patches are blurry, low-frequency yellow blotches. Real goalmouth wear shows bare sandy soil, divots and repaired seams, concentrated in the six-yard box and on the penalty spot. (3) The pitch ends abruptly against farmland: no run-off strip, no edge of artificial surround, no perimeter path or ad-board footings. For a 'desert' or hot-climate theme, the surround should be dry sand, gravel or dead brown grass rather than lush English fields. (4) Net: the checker colours (white and green per the layout) are hard to tell apart; the net reads mostly white with dark hex blotches, and the net sag and back-stanchion shape are barely visible. (5) The corner flag is very small in frame and not judgeable in detail.
suggestions: Add a near-field turf detail layer: a 1-2 m tiling blade normal and albedo-variation map faded in under ~30 m, with grain-direction-dependent roughness so the circle mow keeps showing at low angles.
Give bermuda its own albedo (more yellow-blue, finer) and a slight dry-tip tint for the hot-climate preset; tie the surround to the climate (sand, gravel or dry grass beyond a 3-5 m run-off).
Replace blotchy wear with layered masks: bare sandy soil (albedo ~0.35 tan, roughness 0.95) in the six-yard box and along the keeper's line, divot decals, and lighter wear down the centre channel.
Strengthen the checker net contrast (green cells albedo ~0.08-0.12) and show net sag between the stanchion and the ground bar so the net shape is legible at broadcast distance.
Add a run-off strip and a simple perimeter edge (kerb or path) so the pitch does not end on a hard cut into farmland.
renderer_notes: Detail sheet view 4 is fully black, likely a camera placed inside or below geometry or a failed capture; recapture it. The huge diagonal shadow band in detail view 2 comes from something off-frame (possibly the landscape or a hedgerow at low sun), not from this asset. The lack of turf texture at grazing angles is partly the renderer's grass LOD fade.

summary: Right flat-top tower crane layout and believable lattice mast, but the jib is a flat two-chord ladder, the counter-jib is a bare bar, and the slewing unit, cab, counterweights and trolley are simple boxes.
critique: The overall layout is right for a flat-top crane like the Liebherr 172 EC-B: a square lattice mast on a concrete base, a horizontal jib with a trolley and hook, a short counter-jib with ballast blocks, and a cab at the slewing ring. The mast lattice (chords plus diagonals) reads convincingly at distance. Problems: (1) The jib is a flat ladder: from above (close view) it is just two parallel chords with rungs, and from the side it is a planar zigzag. A real flat-top jib is a triangular-section lattice (two bottom chords that carry the trolley plus one top chord), ~1.0-1.4 m deep, with diagonal lacing on all three faces and tapering at the tip. That triangular shape is the crane's signature silhouette. (2) The counter-jib is a single thin bar with a yellow box and a grey block. It should be a deeper lattice or plated platform with walkway and handrails, the hoist winch drum, the electrical cabinets, and a stack of 3-5 concrete ballast slabs. (3) The slewing unit and cab are a black cube and a yellow box: real cabs are a glazed operator cabin with a floor-to-ceiling front window, mounted to one side of the slewing platform, plus a slewing ring and turntable section. (4) Mast-to-jib proportions: mast height looks roughly equal to jib length (~50-60 m), which is plausible for a free-standing tower, but the mast section looks thin. A 172 EC-B uses a ~1.6-2.0 m square mast with 120 HC sections; check the mast width against the jib depth. (5) Trolley and hook: the trolley is a flat block and the hook block is a small yellow cube. Real hook blocks are a pair of yellow side plates with sheaves and a large red or black hook, and the trolley is a wheeled carriage with sheaves visible under the jib. Use two falls of rope, not one line. (6) No base details: a real crane sits on a reinforced pad with fixing angles or a cross-base with ballast. Also missing are the access ladders and rest platforms inside the mast, the aviation warning light and the anemometer on top, and a site banner on the counter-jib. (7) The material is one flat yellow with no galvanised or primed sections and no grime.
suggestions: Rebuild the jib as a triangular truss: two bottom chords (~100 mm angle or tube) 1.2 m apart, one top chord 1.2 m above, with diagonals on both sides and on the bottom face, tapering in the last section. As line-segment boxes or an alpha-tested lattice card on three faces it stays cheap (~3-5k tris or 3 quads plus a 1k alpha texture).

Counter-jib: a short lattice or plated deck with grey grating, yellow handrails, a hoist winch (drum plus motor box), cabinets, and 4 stacked concrete ballast slabs (~2.5 x 0.6 x 2.0 m each, albedo ~0.5 concrete with stains).

Cab and slewing unit: a glazed operator cab (framed, tinted glass, wiper) on the jib side of the turntable, plus a slewing ring and a short transition section between the mast top and the jib. Add an anemometer and red aviation light on the top.

Trolley and hook: a wheeled trolley visible under the jib bottom chords, two parallel hoist ropes, and a proper hook block (two plate cheeks, sheave, safety-latch hook in red or yellow/black). ~500 tris.
Mast: check the section width (1.6-2.0 m) and add internal ladder rungs plus a rest platform every 2-3 sections. Use an alpha-tested lattice texture on four mast faces for distant LOD.
Base: a 6 x 6 m concrete pad with fixing angles, or a cross-base with ballast blocks, plus a Heras fence ring around it. Add grime on the lower mast and weathering on the ballast.
renderer_notes: The fine lattice aliases and thins out at distance; that is partly the renderer (no MSAA on thin geometry). The mast shadow and the jib shadow look right.
